patterns.name: Who finds it first
patterns.mechanic: The card describes one specific detail at the place (a carved coin, a letter, an odd object in a display); kid and parents race to find it and point at it first. Handicap version: the kid must find N details before a parent finds fewer.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: first to find the gable stone with a golden coin on a quay; Hoorn: first to find the letter H among the VOC letters; Amsterdam: six carved heads before a parent finds three.
variations: Handicap: kid finds 6 before the parent finds 3
Parent searches with one hand over one eye
A model railway lap as the time limit
patterns.fit_notes: Give the kid a fair chance (head start, handicap). Feedback Amsterdam 1.1 (4/5): too easy as a race when the card describes an obvious detail; pick a hidden one or use the handicap. The history behind the detail was the best part.

patterns.name: Read it and translate it
patterns.mechanic: Find words written on a building, gate or monument, read them aloud and work out what they mean (cognates with a language the kid knows, or a parent's help).
patterns.example: Amsterdam: read the warehouse names Vijfhoek, Vierhoek, Driehoek and translate; the Latin words on the zoo gate; three Dutch words on a park temple.
variations: Which word looks like an English one?
Find a word with a number in it and translate the number
patterns.fit_notes: Needs a reader; younger kids can find the letters and a parent reads.

patterns.name: Read the house sign
patterns.mechanic: Find a carved or painted sign (gable stone, inn sign, relief) and answer one question about it: the year on it, what a figure is holding, which animal it shows.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: the year on a tower stone with a woman pointing at a ship; the bird on a brewery sign and what it holds. Hoorn: the biggest ship in a sea-battle frieze and the year on the corner house.
variations: Find the sign from a close-up photo first
How old is it? (subtract with a parent)

patterns.name: Find the number
patterns.mechanic: Find the identifying number or maker's plate on a machine or object (a crane, a locomotive, a tram carriage) and read it off.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: the number on an old harbour crane; the maker's city on the plate inside a historic tram. Hoorn: the steam engine's number, written into a blank on the card.
variations: Fill the number into a blank on the card as a souvenir
patterns.fit_notes: Feedback Amsterdam 7.4 (4/5): seeing the landmark and its history was good, but finding one visible number is too easy for a 7-year-old; add a second step.

patterns.name: Count it
patterns.mechanic: Count one feature of a landmark (animals in a pediment, columns, arches, floors, weights). The parent counts separately; if the numbers differ, count again together pointing with a finger.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: animals in the palace's back pediment; columns in a city gate; balls on a weighted bridge; floors of a round house in the water. Hoorn: arches of the bridge in front of a gate.
variations: Duel: who counts it first
Count standing on one foot
Count only one side, guess the total
patterns.fit_notes: Counting alone is weak; pair it with a question that leads somewhere. Feedback Amsterdam 7.5 (4/5): too easy; and route to a 'wow' landmark from the side where the effect shows (a building rising from the water seen from the water side).

patterns.name: How does it work?
patterns.mechanic: At a machine or moving structure (windmill, drawbridge, lock), find the part that makes it work (the winch, the hinges, the counterweights) and point to it.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: what the miller turns a whole sawmill into the wind with; where the hinges and counterweight balls of a lift bridge are.
variations: Stand where the machine faces you and take a photo
Show the movement with your arms

patterns.name: What lies beneath
patterns.mechanic: Something historic is hidden (a buried canal, an old wall, a former river): find where it shows through (a window in the floor, a grate, a line of different paving).
patterns.example: Hoorn: find where an old canal under a church square can be seen, and whether there is water in it.
variations: Walk the line of the old wall in the paving

patterns.name: Riddle to the next stop
patterns.mechanic: A riddle or hint describes the next landmark without naming it (its look, the street's name); the kid leads the family there and proves arrival with a count or a number read on the spot.
patterns.example: Hoorn: find the gate with a prince on its roof in the 'newest' street, then count the coats of arms. Amsterdam: through a gate into a hidden courtyard, find the number of the oldest wooden house.
variations: Hint by street-name meaning
Follow a symbol on street signs

patterns.name: Which way?
patterns.mechanic: Timed: the kid runs round a square reading the street signs and stands at the street or alley that leads to a named place.
patterns.example: Hoorn: in 2 minutes, find the alley from the main square to the harbour.
variations: Use the street-name meaning as the hint
patterns.fit_notes: Only on a square without traffic.

patterns.name: Zone photo hunt
patterns.mechanic: A list of the zone's sights (or a category: boats of three companies, three towers) to photograph while walking, any order, before the boss. Each target is on the zone map; one coin per target.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: 5–6 camera-marked sights per zone (towers, a palace, a statue, a market), plus boats of three different companies.
variations: Hunt a category instead of named spots
Sights + a category together
patterns.fit_notes: Make it the zone's first challenge; no timer.

patterns.name: Window bingo
patterns.mechanic: During a ride, a list of things to see from the window (a farm type, a windmill, a tower, a named building); point and shout or photograph; any N of M wins.
patterns.example: Hoorn: from a steam tram, 3 of 4 (pyramid-roofed farm, windmill, church tower, sheep). Amsterdam: from a ferry, photograph 4 of 6 harbour sights.
variations: Photo version for moving sights
Duel: who shouts first

patterns.name: Count the stops
patterns.mechanic: The kid checks in and counts the stops to the destination, and photographs a vehicle of the same line going the other way.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: tram from the central station, count stops, photo of the oncoming tram.
variations: Guess the number of stops first
patterns.fit_notes: Feedback Amsterdam 7.1 (5/5): spotting a passing tram is luck-dependent (the first one came near the last stop); give a fallback (the return ride, the stop).

patterns.name: Guess, then count
patterns.mechanic: Everyone guesses a number (bridges on an island, whistles in 10 minutes, how many houses tall a shaft is); then count or look it up on the spot; closest guess wins.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: how many bridges on an island, then walk and count; how many canal houses stacked would reach the street from a deep metro station. Hoorn: whistles of a steam engine in the first 10 minutes.
variations: Guess in body units
Check with a sign or the parent page
patterns.fit_notes: Feedback Amsterdam 7.2 (5/5): counting something spread over the whole area (bridges on an island) makes the family explore it, and the guess makes it a competition. Strong pattern.

patterns.name: Pace it and compare
patterns.mechanic: Pace or arm-span a small thing (a narrow house, one house in a row, a bridge deck), then use it to work out something bigger you can see (the whole row, the big house opposite, the raised bridge's height); check by walking or with a known number.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: pace one captain's house, predict the row of 13, walk to check; how many door-wide houses fit in the merchant house opposite (guess duel). Hoorn: pace a drawbridge's lifting deck, how many of you stacked reach its tip when raised.
variations: Guess duel before measuring
Use arm spans instead of steps
patterns.fit_notes: The kid's step and arm span come from the family's measures field. Feedback Amsterdam 1.2 (4/5): a kid's steps change size while counting and walking at once, so totals don't match; let a parent count while the kid walks, or pace heel-to-toe.

patterns.name: Caterpillar measure
patterns.mechanic: Make an old or big unit of length tangible: a parent marks one unit out, the kid lies down repeatedly like a caterpillar along it; how many kids long is it?
patterns.example: Amsterdam: a windmill named after its distance in an old unit (a 'roe', ~3.7 m); the kid measures one roe lying down.
variations: Use a fathom (arm span) or a foot
patterns.fit_notes: Needs grass or clean ground.

patterns.name: Perspective trick
patterns.mechanic: Walk away from a big landmark until it lines up with the kid's body (on the palm, on a fingertip, as a crown on the head, behind a fingernail); a parent takes the photo. Slipped off? Move and shoot again.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: a tower's crown on the kid's head; a crane hotel on the palm; a golden lyre on a fingertip; a ship-shaped house 'sailing' towards the camera. Hoorn: a red unicorn hidden behind a little fingernail.
variations: Frame a building so it moves toward you
Add: count the hour's bell strikes and jump that many times
patterns.fit_notes: Good boss when retakes are expected.

patterns.name: Animals in one frame
patterns.mechanic: Photograph live animals: two different species in one frame, or a zoo animal seen from outside the fence.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: two different water birds in one photo on an island quay; a giraffe or zebra seen across the canal from the zoo's savannah.
variations: Three species
A bird in flight
patterns.fit_notes: Feedback Amsterdam 1.3 (4/5): depends on luck (few birds in November); name a backup spot with reliable animals.

patterns.name: The scariest one
patterns.mechanic: A building or room is full of carvings; the kid looks at all of them and photographs the one that fits a prompt (scariest, funniest, strangest), explaining why.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: the scariest stone sea monster on a shipping house.
variations: Parents guess which one the kid picked
patterns.fit_notes: Open-ended; the proof is the photo.

patterns.name: Statue twin
patterns.mechanic: Stand next to a statue and copy its pose and expression so the photo looks like twins.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: twin pose with a bronze street-urchin statue on a square.
variations: Parents rate the likeness 1–10
Copy a statue the parents choose

patterns.name: Freeze like a statue
patterns.mechanic: Freeze in a statue's pose for 30 seconds while a parent tries to make the kid laugh without touching. Laugh or move: start again.
patterns.example: Hoorn: next to three bronze ship's boys, become the fourth.
variations: Swap: the parent freezes
patterns.fit_notes: Boss level.

patterns.name: Playground circuit
patterns.mechanic: Timed: touch N different play items, visit 5 chosen ones, or repeat one (a slide) N times within a minute or three; a parent times and counts.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: touch 15 things in 1 minute; climb/sit/swing on 5 chosen things in 2 minutes; the slide 10 times in 3 minutes.
variations: Beat your record
Only red things
patterns.fit_notes: Use where a zone needs a breather. Feedback Amsterdam 1.4 (4/5): scale the target to the playground; a small toddler playground made it trivial (done in half the time). Feedback Amsterdam 7.3 (5/5): park-like playground with little equipment, 5 items barely found; the kid loved running anyway. 'N different things to climb, ride or play on' is more fun than just touching things, so keep it; the problem was too little equipment. Check what the playground has (photos, OSM) and set N to fit it.

patterns.name: Lap the landmark
patterns.mechanic: Run all the way round a free-standing building in a time limit, counting something on the way, or rest and beat the first time.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: run round a cross-shaped church in 2 minutes counting the little houses in its corners; run round a round gas holder and beat your record.
patterns.fit_notes: Only where the path round is traffic-free.

patterns.name: Race the boat
patterns.mechanic: Time the kid over a known distance and compare with something that moves there (a rowing boat, a tram); race it if one passes.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: run 100 m along a rowing course; a rowing eight does it in under 20 s.

patterns.name: Stairs on the clock
patterns.mechanic: Time the kid on the stairs (or the lift) of a tall building, compare with the kid's own one-floor time or the lift, then try to beat it.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: climb to a museum roof, how many floors, then run up again a floor faster.
variations: Lift is N times faster than you

patterns.name: Find it from above
patterns.mechanic: From a high point or on a city model, find and point to 3–4 places already visited, in a time limit. Too slow: a parent names new ones, sometimes with one eye covered.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: from a tower top, point to the station, a museum, a tower crown and a crane hotel in 3 minutes; on a huge city model, find 4 places already conquered in 2 minutes.
variations: With one eye covered
Time the lift first
patterns.fit_notes: Boss when places are far apart.

patterns.name: Team interpreter
patterns.mechanic: The kid orders or asks a staff member a question in the local language and translates what was said for the family.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: order apple pie and ask how many they bake a day; ask a miller how the sails stand at a party, then show it with the arms. Hoorn: ask a costumed helper what the saint's horse is called.
variations: Add a pose: show the answer with your body and hold it
patterns.fit_notes: Only where staff are reliably present.

patterns.name: The venue's own trail
patterns.mechanic: Pick up the venue's own kids' trail, stamp card or search sheet at the desk and finish it; add one extra live find inside.
patterns.example: Hoorn: the search sheet at a LEGO-brick attraction. Amsterdam: a microbe museum's stamp card (12 stamps) plus a live water bear; a street-art hall's kids' treasure hunt asked for at the desk.
variations: Time limit for a boss
patterns.fit_notes: Check the venue really has one.

patterns.name: Exhibit with an answer
patterns.mechanic: Use or find a named exhibit and bring back one concrete answer (name 5 kinds of something shown, the reading on an interactive device).
patterns.example: Amsterdam: walk into a whale model and name 5 kinds of sea rubbish in the last room; use a kiss-o-meter and a microbe mirror.
patterns.fit_notes: Put the room name in the answer.

patterns.name: Inside the painting
patterns.mechanic: In front of a famous painting, find small details in it (a figure, an animal) and point at them.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: in a famous group portrait, find the girl with a chicken on her belt and the barking dog.
variations: Parents ask why it has its name

patterns.name: Look and remember
patterns.mechanic: Look at a detailed object (a doll's house, a shop window, a model) for one minute, turn away, answer 5 questions from a parent; 4 right wins, otherwise look again with new questions.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: a historic doll's house in a big museum.
variations: Kid asks the parents
Kim's game: parent covers part of a shop window with a hand; what's missing?
patterns.fit_notes: Boss-level.

patterns.name: Where is this?
patterns.mechanic: A parent secretly photographs 3 close-up details of a building; the kid has a time limit to find where each is and answer one question about it.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: carved details over the guild doors of a weigh house; say which guild worked behind each.
variations: New photos if too slow
In a gallery: describe or photograph a small detail of a painting, kids find the painting

sources.title: Wherever Family: museum games to play with kids

patterns.name: Captain's orders
patterns.mechanic: A parent names N places or objects once; the kid visits them in exactly that order within a time limit; a mistake gives a new order.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: on a replica ship, the wheel, bell, hammock, cannon and captain's cabin in 3 minutes.
variations: 7 places for a boss

patterns.name: Where is north?
patterns.mechanic: Everyone stands where they think north is (at a wind rose, a sundial, a compass in the paving); check with a phone compass; closest wins.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: under a glass roof drawn like a wind rose in a maritime museum's courtyard.

patterns.name: Spot it at the event
patterns.mechanic: At a parade or arrival, find 3 items before a moment (the boat's name, a figure on the mast, the horse), then shout a local greeting.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: Sinterklaas's steamboat arrival; find its name, a Piet on the mast and the white horse before it ties up.
patterns.fit_notes: Date-bound; give a fallback task.

patterns.name: Animal charades
patterns.mechanic: The kid acts out N animals seen there without sounds; parents must guess at least a threshold.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: 5 animals at a city farm, parents guess at least 3.
patterns.fit_notes: Co-op with a threshold, not a duel. Feedback Amsterdam 1.5 (5/5): say that each animal must be guessed at the first attempt.

patterns.name: Walk like a…
patterns.mechanic: Cover a set distance in a funny gait tied to the place (ostrich knees high, human wheelbarrow) within a time limit; normal walking or a fall means start again.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: ostrich steps to a tree near a windmill brewery with an ostrich sign; a human wheelbarrow at a forest built with wheelbarrows.
variations: Crab walk
Penguin waddle

patterns.name: Cross it the hard way
patterns.mechanic: Cross a bridge, stairs or a building front under a limitation with a fail condition: eyes closed without touching the railings, walking backwards holding the rail, heel to toe balancing objects on open palms. Fail: start again.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: cross a numbered bridge eyes closed; back over a snake bridge walking backwards. Hoorn: 'living scales' along a weigh house with a glove on each palm.
variations: Count the steps on the way
One hand behind your back
patterns.fit_notes: Boss pattern. Parent walks behind; only when no bikes come. Feedback Amsterdam 1.B (5/5, zone favourite): took 3 attempts, fun and challenging; tying it to the bridge's name, place and history made it. Feedback Amsterdam 7.B (5/5): physical, failable and hard enough even when done on the first attempt (walking backwards down stairs holding the rail).

patterns.name: Sing on one foot
patterns.mechanic: Perform a local song or rhyme in full standing on one foot; foot down or a mistake means start again.
patterns.example: Hoorn: sing a Sinterklaas song at a steam-tram stop.

patterns.name: Windmill arms
patterns.mechanic: Mimic a moving thing with the body in its rhythm (sails turning); drop an arm or lose the beat and you're out; last one going wins.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: arms as windmill sails in time with the real sails.
variations: No wind: to a parent's count
patterns.fit_notes: Clear, safe end condition.

patterns.name: Shuttle run
patterns.mechanic: Run between two points N times in a time limit, or carry N found items one at a time to a spot; duel version: parent does the same.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: under a container arch and back 5 times in a minute. Hoorn: carry 5 different leaves ('powder bags') one at a time to a bench by a powder tower.

patterns.name: Blind tasting
patterns.mechanic: Eyes closed, a parent gives pieces of 2–5 local foods in any order; name each. Duel: swap and compare scores. Or taste first, then find the names in the stall window.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: two fries sauces (duel); 5 chocolate flavours, 4 right; two kinds of winter doughnut, then find their names at the stall.
variations: Find the names on the price list afterwards

patterns.name: Taste, name and rate
patterns.mechanic: Try a local food, find its local name (or an ingredient word) on a sign at the stand, and rate it 1–10; optionally count or decorate.
patterns.example: Hoorn: fried fish bites, find the fish's name by the counter. Amsterdam: goat's milk at a farm café and the word for goat on a sign; pancake boat, count pancakes and decorate one with the city flag.

patterns.name: Brick build with a test
patterns.mechanic: At a brick store's demo table or a brick attraction, build to a spec with a stress test (taller than your elbow and survives being blown on; a gate a toy car drives through and stands 5 s).
patterns.example: Amsterdam: tower from 4 kinds of pieces at a LEGO store. Hoorn: a gate with a house on top at a brick museum.
variations: Copy a landmark seen that day
patterns.fit_notes: At most one per campaign.

patterns.name: Build from what fell
patterns.mechanic: Build from fallen sticks, bark and leaves to a test: a den that stands alone 10 s, a boat that floats 10 s with a passenger.
patterns.example: Amsterdam: a round den shaped like a gas holder on a wild island; a stick boat with an acorn passenger at a forest's play islands.
variations: Timed collection first
patterns.fit_notes: Only fallen material.

patterns.name: Secret word
patterns.mechanic: Each challenge's answer has one marked letter (a circled box on the card); the kid collects the letters through the zone or day, and at the end they spell a secret word that unlocks the finale or the medal.
patterns.example: An Austrian town's kids' rally has answer boxes at every station, a few circled; the circled letters give the solution word handed in at the tourist office. A Dutch party-hunt idea uses a secret-code key sheet in the same way.
variations: The word is the name of the zone's boss landmark
Letters come in jumbled order: unscramble
Younger kids: collect stickers with letters instead of writing
patterns.fit_notes: Writes letters only into ready boxes; works as the zone's thread across challenges. Type 'collect' with no physical object: the letters are the collection.

patterns.name: How high was the water?
patterns.mechanic: Find a high-water mark (a plaque or line with a year) on a gate, wall or church; read the year, stand under it and work out how many of you, stacked up, the water reached; or where it would reach on a parent.
patterns.example: An Austrian rally asks for the year on the water-level mark by the old town gate; we turn it into a body measurement on the spot.
variations: Mark the kid's height with a hand and compare
Several marks: which flood was the worst?
patterns.fit_notes: Changed from 'read the year' to a body comparison so the number leads somewhere (challenge-design §1).

patterns.name: Weathervane
patterns.mechanic: Find the figure on the very top of a tower (a rooster, a ship, a knight, an animal) and name it; then say which way the wind is blowing from where it points, and check with flags, smoke or a wet finger.
patterns.example: A kids' city rally asks which animal sits on top of a cathedral's bell tower and the name of the little knight in another church tower.
variations: Duel: who names the figure first
Point to where the wind comes from with eyes closed, then check
patterns.fit_notes: Needs binoculars or a zoomed phone photo on tall towers.

patterns.name: Rubbing for the collection
patterns.mechanic: Put paper on a relief (a manhole cover with the city's arms, a brass plaque, a waymark, a tree bark) and rub a crayon over it until the pattern shows; the rubbing goes into the collection.
patterns.example: A town park has a brass-rubbing trail of plaques on waymark posts; a craft blog collects city manhole-cover designs as rubbings, photographing the cover first and brushing off grit.
variations: Find 3 different manhole covers in the zone
Rubbing of a coin bought at a museum shop
patterns.fit_notes: Needs a wax crayon (not in the needs list) and a thin paper card; only on relief you may touch.

patterns.name: Price bingo
patterns.mechanic: The card has a small grid of prices (50 c, 1, 2, 3, 5); at a market or shop the kid finds one item per price and names it in the local language from the label.
patterns.example: A money-skills blog gives kids a printed board of price points to fill while walking through a store.
variations: Buy the cheapest local fruit with exact coins
Find the most expensive thing per kilo

sources.title: Money Prodigy: grocery store scavenger hunt

patterns.name: Guess the weight
patterns.mechanic: Everyone holds the same fruit, cheese or bag of sweets and guesses its weight; it goes on the stall's scale; closest guess wins (and the family buys it).
patterns.example: A children's health charity's grocery hunt has kids pick produce, weigh it and estimate its price from the weight.
variations: Guess the price instead
Kid picks the piece closest to 500 g
patterns.fit_notes: Only at stalls with a visible scale; ask the vendor.

sources.title: Action for Healthy Kids: grocery scavenger hunt

patterns.name: One minute of silence
patterns.mechanic: Stand still with eyes closed for one minute and listen; then name all the different sounds heard (bells, gulls, a tram, a language). Reach a target number, or tick off a short checklist of sounds the place should have.
patterns.example: Speech-therapy and nature-education guides take children on listening walks, stopping to name sounds and give them words (brmm, whoosh), with a checklist of cars, bells, voices.
variations: Duel: kid vs parent, who hears more
Sound checklist made for the place: a carillon, a tram bell, a market call
patterns.fit_notes: Proof: kid says each sound, a parent counts. Best where the place has a signature sound.

patterns.name: Which place was that?
patterns.mechanic: At several stops the kid secretly records 10 seconds of sound with the phone (no picture); later, at lunch or the boss, the parents listen and must guess which stop each one is; kid wins for each wrong guess.
patterns.example: A listening-walk guide suggests recording the sounds at each stopping point and replaying them later for the children to name.
variations: Swap: parents record, kid guesses
Record inside a church, a station and a market
patterns.fit_notes: Changed to a duel with parents guessing so it has a clear winner.

patterns.name: Mason's marks
patterns.mechanic: Search the stone blocks of an old church, tower or wall for stonemasons' marks (small carved signs: arrows, crosses, letters); find N different ones, or find the one shown on the card.
patterns.example: A historic-churches children's trail asks kids to look for the mason's mark on the wall near a church porch and the skull and crossbones on stones by a door.
variations: Make up your own mark: which one would you carve?
Where is the lowest / highest mark?
patterns.fit_notes: Check on site or in photos that marks are visible at kid height.

sources.title: Norwich Historic Churches Trust: Angels and Dragons children's trail

patterns.name: One foot in each
patterns.mechanic: Find a boundary marker (parish plaque, old city-limit stone, district line in the paving, border on a bridge) and stand with one foot on each side for a photo; say what the two sides are.
patterns.example: A children's church trail asks kids to spot the parish boundary plaques and say what they tell you.
variations: Find both plaques of the same boundary
Jump from one side to the other 10 times
patterns.fit_notes: Made into a body pose so it needs being there.

sources.title: Norwich Historic Churches Trust: Angels and Dragons children's trail

patterns.name: Count them all day
patterns.mechanic: A motif is chosen for the zone (lions, angels, dragons, the city arms, bikes with a child seat); everyone guesses how many they will see; the kid keeps a running tally on the card while walking, and the closest guess wins at the boss.
patterns.example: A city church trail asks: how many angels and dragons can you spot on this whole trail? with tally boxes on the leaflet.
variations: Two motifs, kid counts one, parents the other
Only motifs higher than a door
patterns.fit_notes: Like the zone photo hunt: runs alongside the other challenges, no clock.

sources.title: Norwich Historic Churches Trust: Angels and Dragons children's trail

patterns.name: Where is this photo from?
patterns.mechanic: The next stop is given only as a photo of a familiar object from an unusual angle or very close up (a lamp from below, a bench's ironwork, a door handle); the kid leads the family there and retakes the same photo.
patterns.example: A Russian education blog's quick outdoor quest: every clue is a photo of an everyday object shot from an unfamiliar angle, leading to the next point.
variations: Two photos: the near one and a far one, choose
Kid takes the next photo for the parents
patterns.fit_notes: Different from close-up-match: here the photo moves the family through the zone.

sources.title: Mel.fm: 4 ideas for a street quest prepared in half an hour

patterns.name: Then and now
patterns.mechanic: The card shows an old photograph or painting of a spot in the zone; the kid finds the exact place it was taken from, retakes the same view, and finds 3 things that changed and 1 that stayed.
patterns.example: Heritage teaching guides have pupils compare old photographs with the street itself and match historic photos with today's view; a St Petersburg self-guided kids' quest uses retro photos as clues.
variations: Old painting from a museum seen that morning
Stand where the painter stood
patterns.fit_notes: Check rights for printing the old image; public-domain archive photos are best.

sources.title: Derbyshire Record Office: using old photographs
Oswego Heritage Council: Then & Now lesson

patterns.name: Meet it blind
patterns.mechanic: A parent leads the blindfolded (eyes-closed) kid to one tree, column, lamp post or statue base among many; the kid explores it by touch and smell, is led back on a winding route, opens their eyes and must find the same one.
patterns.example: Forest-school 'Meet a Tree': the guide leads the blindfolded partner to a tree, back to the start, and the partner finds the tree by what they felt; an outdoor centre adds guessing the tree's girth.
variations: Swap: the kid leads a parent
Columns in a church colonnade or a row of plane trees on a square
Guess the trunk's girth in hugs
patterns.fit_notes: Kid walks slowly, hands forward, a parent holds them; only in a car-free spot.

sources.title: Notts Outdoors: Mega Messy Maths (tree girth)

patterns.name: How tall? Ask the shadow
patterns.mechanic: On a sunny day, pace the kid's own shadow and the shadow of a tower, statue or lamp post; the shadow is as many times longer as the thing is taller than the kid, so work out its height and compare with the real number.
patterns.example: Park-service and school number-day activities measure a person's height and shadow, then a building's shadow, and solve the proportion; younger kids use a 1 m stick.
variations: Younger kids: how many 'of my shadow' fit in the tower's shadow
Do it at two times of day
patterns.fit_notes: Needs sun and a shadow that falls on open ground; give the real height in the answer.

patterns.name: Rock-paper-scissors stairs
patterns.mechanic: Kid and a parent start at the bottom of a staircase and play rock-paper-scissors; the winner climbs 3 steps for rock and 6 for scissors or paper, spelling a word one syllable per step; first to the top wins.
patterns.example: A Japanese street game promoted by a confectioner: players advance across squares or steps by the number of syllables of the winning hand's word.
variations: Use a local word: 3 syllables for rock, 6 for the others
Going down: the loser goes back 1 step
patterns.fit_notes: Only on quiet, wide steps; luck-based, so fair for small kids.

sources.title: Glico teacher file: the Glico game

patterns.name: Letters of my name
patterns.mechanic: Find and photograph each letter of the kid's name in the zone, each from a different sign, house number or shape in a building (an A in a roof, an O in a window); later the photos spell the name.
patterns.example: A design magazine's 'big letter hunt' and a library's 'how to be a building' activity have children spot letters hidden in architecture and photograph every letter they find.
variations: Only letters in buildings, not signs
Spell the city's name instead
patterns.fit_notes: Runs through the zone like a photo hunt; the letter photos are a collection.

sources.title: AIGA Eye on Design: the big letter hunt
Chicago Public Library: How to be a building

patterns.name: Map in your head
patterns.mechanic: A parent stays at the middle of a square or park with a map; the kid looks at one marked spot on it, leaves the map behind, goes there and brings back a word or number from that spot; then the next spot, from the centre each time.
patterns.example: Orienteering lesson plans for children: 'star' courses from a central point, and a memory variant where the map stays at the start and children must remember where the control is.
variations: Kid memorises two spots in a row
Parent times the whole star
patterns.fit_notes: Only within sight of the parent, in a car-free square or park.

sources.title: Brighton & Hove: orienteering exercises for schools

patterns.name: Shape hunt
patterns.mechanic: In one building or square, find and photograph a list of shapes: a circle, a triangle, a star, a spiral, an octagon (count the sides of a font or a tower); proof is the photo plus the side count.
patterns.example: Outdoor-maths teachers run geometry hunts with checklists of shapes to photograph; church trails ask how many sides the font has.
variations: Find the shape with the most sides
A shape that is in the city's coat of arms

patterns.name: Mascot's day out
patterns.mechanic: A small toy travels with the kid; at each landmark the kid places it in a scene that fits the place (on a bridge rail, by a statue's foot, in a market crate) and photographs it; at the end of the day the photos are put in order as the mascot's story.
patterns.example: A German early-years card set has children take invented figures outside, find exciting places for them, photograph each station and sort the photos into a picture-book story.
variations: The mascot must 'meet' 3 animals (statues count)
Parents choose the best scene of the day
patterns.fit_notes: Toy must stay safe from canals.

patterns.name: Which painting am I?
patterns.mechanic: In a gallery room, the kid secretly picks a painting or sculpture and strikes the pose of one figure in it; the parents must find which artwork it is within a set time; then swap.
patterns.example: Family art-gallery games: pose like a subject in a work of art and have the others guess which work you are.
variations: Parents get 3 guesses
Only works with animals in them
patterns.fit_notes: Quiet poses only; no touching artworks.

sources.title: LDS Living: art gallery games for families

patterns.name: Departure board race
patterns.mechanic: At a big station's departure board, a parent names a far city; the kid and the other parent race to find the train's time and platform, then walk to that platform and find the sign or the train.
patterns.example: Invented from station I-spy books (points for spotting the departure board) and timetable lessons.
variations: Find a train that leaves within 10 minutes
Which train goes furthest? Guess, then check on the map
patterns.fit_notes: Only walk onto platforms with a valid ticket or where they are public.

patterns.name: Echo hunt
patterns.mechanic: Clap once under a bridge, in a gate passage or a big hall and listen for the echo; find the spot in the zone with the longest or loudest echo, and compare: here vs. there.
patterns.example: Invented from the listening-walk sources: a sound task with a measurable comparison.
variations: In a church only whisper a word and listen how long it hangs (no clapping)
Count seconds until the sound dies
patterns.fit_notes: Respect quiet places: in churches only listen to existing sounds.

patterns.name: Find the middle
patterns.mechanic: Everyone stands where they think the exact centre of a square is; then the kid paces from two opposite sides (and the other two) to check whose spot is the middle; closest wins.
patterns.example: Invented from a symmetry/centre-finding maths note (diagonals meet in the middle) and our guess-then-check duels.
variations: Find the centre of a round fountain
Eyes closed: walk to the centre from one corner
patterns.fit_notes: Only on a car-free square.

patterns.name: Mini landmark
patterns.mechanic: Build a small copy of the landmark in front of you (a windmill, a bridge, a tower) from what lies on the ground (sticks, stones, leaves); photograph it with the real one behind it in the same frame.
patterns.example: Invented: combines our found-materials builds with the perspective-trick photo.
variations: Parents must say which landmark it is before seeing the real one
It must stand for 10 seconds
patterns.fit_notes: Only fallen material.
